title: Germs and Handwashing
summary: What germs are, how they spread from hands to bodies, how soap and water remove them, and how and when to wash your hands.
poll: Washing your hands is the most important thing you can do to stay healthy.

versions.title: Wash Away the Germs
versions.text:
Look at your hands. They look clean. But they may have germs!

Germs are tiny. They are so small that you can not see them. Some germs are good. Some do no harm. But some germs can make you sick. They can give you a cold or a sore tummy.

How do germs get on you? You touch a door. You touch a toy. Germs from it get on your hands. Then you rub your eyes or touch your mouth. The germs get in. A cough or a sneeze can spread germs, too.

You can stop them. Wash your hands with soap and water! Soap grabs the germs. It lifts them off your skin. Then the water takes them away.

Here is how to do it. Get your hands wet. Put on soap. Scrub all of your hands, the backs too. Scrub as long as it takes to sing a short song two times. Rinse. Dry with a clean towel.

When should you wash? Wash when you eat. Wash when you use the toilet. Wash when you come in from play. No soap? Hand gel can help. When you cough, cough in your arm.

versions.title: Wash Away the Germs
versions.text:
Look at your hands. They may look clean. But they may be covered with germs!

Germs are tiny living things. They are so small that you can not see them with just your eyes. Many germs do no harm. Some even help us. But some germs can make you sick. They can give you a cold, the flu, or a sore tummy.

How do germs get on you? You touch a door handle or a toy. Germs from it stick to your hands. Then you rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth. Now the germs can get inside you. When people cough or sneeze, they spread germs into the air, too.

The good news is that you can stop germs. Just wash your hands with soap and water! Soap grabs the germs and lifts them off your skin. Then the water washes them away.

Here is how. First, wet your hands. Next, put on soap. Then scrub all parts of your hands, even the backs and between your fingers. Scrub for twenty seconds. That is as long as singing a short song two times. Last, rinse and dry with a clean towel.

When should you wash? Wash before you eat. Wash after you use the toilet. Wash after you play outside. If there is no soap, hand gel can help. And always cough or sneeze into your elbow.

versions.title: Germs and Handwashing
versions.text:
Take a look at your hands. They might look clean, but they could be covered with thousands of germs!

Germs are tiny living things. They are so small that you cannot see them with just your eyes. Many germs are harmless, and some even help our bodies. But some germs can make us sick. They can cause colds, the flu, and stomach aches.

How do germs get into your body? When you touch a door handle, a toy, or a phone, germs can stick to your skin. Then, if you rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, the germs can get inside. When people cough or sneeze, they also spread germs into the air in tiny drops.

The good news is that you can stop germs from spreading. One of the best ways is simply to wash your hands with soap and water. Soap grabs germs and dirt and pulls them off your skin. Then the running water rinses them down the drain.

Here is how to wash the right way. First, wet your hands with clean water. Next, add soap. Then scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, between your fingers, and under your nails. Scrub for at least twenty seconds, which is about as long as singing a short song twice. Finally, rinse well and dry your hands with a clean towel.

Wash your hands before you eat, after you use the toilet, and after you play outside or touch animals. If there is no soap and water, hand gel can help. And always cough or sneeze into your elbow instead of your hands.

versions.title: Germs and Handwashing
versions.text:
Take a close look at your hands. They might look perfectly clean, but they could be covered with thousands of germs that are too small to see.

Germs are tiny living things. To see them, you would need a microscope. It is a tool that makes very small things look much larger. There are different kinds of germs, such as bacteria and viruses. Many bacteria are harmless, and some even help our bodies digest food. However, some germs can make us sick with colds, the flu, or stomach illnesses.

Germs spread easily. When you touch a door handle, a toy, or any other surface, germs can stick to your skin. If you then rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, the germs can enter your body. When people cough or sneeze, they also spray tiny drops full of germs into the air.

The good news is that one of the best ways to stop germs is also one of the simplest. Washing your hands with soap and water removes many germs. Soap grabs germs and dirt and loosens them from your skin. Then the running water can rinse them away.

To wash the right way, first wet your hands with clean water and add soap. Then scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, between your fingers, and under your nails. Keep scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, which is about as long as singing a short song twice. Finally, rinse well and dry your hands with a clean towel.

Wash your hands before you eat, after you use the toilet, and after you play outside or touch animals. When soap and water are not available, a hand gel made with alcohol can help. Also, cough or sneeze into your elbow instead of your hands.

About 175 years ago, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that fewer patients got sick when doctors washed their hands. Today, handwashing is one of the most important habits in every hospital.

versions.title: The Science of Handwashing
versions.text:
Your hands might appear perfectly clean, but they could be carrying thousands of germs that are far too small to detect with the naked eye.

Germs are microorganisms, which are living things so small that observing them requires a microscope, an instrument that makes extremely tiny objects appear much larger. The two most familiar categories of germs are bacteria and viruses. Many bacteria are harmless, and some even assist our bodies in digesting food; nevertheless, certain germs can cause an infection, producing illnesses such as colds, influenza, or stomach upsets.

The transmission of germs from one person to another happens remarkably easily. When you touch a door handle, a toy, or any other surface, germs can attach to your skin. If you subsequently rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, those germs can enter your body. Additionally, when people cough or sneeze, they release tiny droplets containing germs into the surrounding air.

Fortunately, one of the most effective methods for preventing infection is also one of the simplest. Washing your hands with soap and water removes many harmful germs. Each soap molecule has one end that is attracted to water and another end that attaches to oils and dirt, so soap loosens germs from your skin and allows running water to rinse them away.

To wash properly, first moisten your hands with clean water and apply soap. Then scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, the spaces between your fingers, and the area underneath your nails. Continue scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, which is approximately as long as singing a short song twice. Finally, rinse thoroughly and dry your hands with a clean towel.

Wash your hands before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing outdoors or handling animals. When soap and water are unavailable, a hand sanitizer containing alcohol can provide some protection. In addition, cough or sneeze into your elbow rather than your hands.

Approximately 175 years ago, a Hungarian doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis observed that significantly fewer patients became seriously ill when doctors washed their hands. Although many doctors initially rejected his conclusion, handwashing is now considered one of the most essential practices in hospitals throughout the world.

versions.title: The Science of Handwashing
versions.text:
Your hands might appear perfectly clean, but they could be carrying thousands of germs that are far too small to detect with the naked eye.

Germs are microorganisms, which are living things so minuscule that observing them requires a microscope, an instrument that magnifies extremely tiny objects. The two most familiar categories of germs are bacteria and viruses. Many bacteria are harmless, and some even assist our bodies in digesting food; nevertheless, certain germs can cause an infection, producing illnesses such as colds, influenza, or stomach upsets.

The transmission of germs from one person to another occurs remarkably easily. When you touch a door handle, a toy, or any other surface, germs can attach themselves to your skin, and if you subsequently rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, those germs can enter your body. Additionally, whenever people cough or sneeze, they release tiny droplets containing germs into the surrounding air.

Fortunately, one of the most effective methods for preventing infection is also one of the simplest: washing your hands with soap and water. Each soap molecule has one end that is attracted to water and another end that attaches to oils and dirt, so soap loosens germs from your skin and enables running water to rinse them away.

To wash effectively, moisten your hands with clean water, apply soap, and scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, the spaces between your fingers, and the area underneath your fingernails. Continue scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, which is approximately as long as singing a short song twice, and then rinse thoroughly and dry your hands with a clean towel.

Wash your hands before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing outdoors or handling animals. When soap and water are unavailable, a hand sanitizer containing alcohol can provide some protection, although it is less effective on visibly dirty hands. In addition, cough or sneeze into your elbow rather than your hands.

Approximately 175 years ago, a Hungarian physician named Ignaz Semmelweis observed that significantly fewer patients became seriously ill when doctors washed their hands. Although many of his colleagues initially rejected his conclusion, handwashing is now considered one of the most essential practices in hospitals throughout the world.

versions.title: The Science of Handwashing
versions.text:
Your hands might appear perfectly clean, but they could be carrying thousands of germs that are far too small to detect with the naked eye.

Germs are microorganisms, which are living things so minuscule that observing them requires a microscope, an instrument that magnifies extremely tiny objects. The two most familiar categories of germs are bacteria and viruses. Many bacteria are harmless, and some even assist our bodies in digesting food; nevertheless, certain germs can cause an infection, producing illnesses such as colds, influenza, or digestive disorders.

The transmission of germs from one person to another occurs remarkably easily. When you touch a door handle, a toy, or any other contaminated surface, germs can attach themselves to your skin, and if you subsequently rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, those germs can enter your body. Additionally, whenever people cough or sneeze, they release microscopic droplets containing germs into the surrounding atmosphere.

Fortunately, one of the most effective methods for preventing infection is also one of the simplest: washing your hands with soap and water. Each soap molecule has one end that is attracted to water and another end that attaches to oils and dirt, so soap loosens germs from your skin and enables running water to rinse them away. Soap can even dismantle the protective outer layer surrounding certain viruses, which effectively destroys them.

To wash effectively, moisten your hands with clean water, apply soap, and scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, the spaces between your fingers, and the area underneath your fingernails. Continue scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, which is approximately as long as singing a short song twice, and then rinse thoroughly and dry your hands with a clean towel.

You should wash your hands before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing outdoors or handling animals. When soap and water are unavailable, a hand sanitizer containing alcohol can provide some protection, although it is considerably less effective on visibly dirty hands. In addition, coughing or sneezing into your elbow rather than your hands reduces the contamination of everything you subsequently touch.

Approximately 175 years ago, a Hungarian physician named Ignaz Semmelweis observed that significantly fewer patients became seriously ill when doctors washed their hands. Although many of his colleagues initially rejected his conclusion, handwashing is now considered one of the most essential practices in hospitals throughout the world.

versions.title: The Science of Handwashing
versions.text:
Your hands might appear perfectly clean, but they could be carrying thousands of germs that are far too small to detect with the naked eye.

Germs are microorganisms, which are living things so minuscule that observing them requires a microscope, an instrument that magnifies extremely tiny objects, and the two most familiar categories of germs are bacteria and viruses. Numerous bacteria are harmless, and some even assist our bodies in digesting food; nevertheless, certain germs can cause an infection, producing illnesses such as colds, influenza, or digestive disorders.

The transmission of germs from one individual to another occurs remarkably easily. When you touch a door handle, a toy, or any other contaminated surface, germs can attach themselves to your skin, and if you subsequently rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth, those germs can enter your body. Additionally, whenever infected people cough or sneeze, they release microscopic droplets containing germs into the surrounding atmosphere, where other people may inhale them.

Fortunately, one of the most effective methods for preventing infection is also one of the simplest: washing your hands with soap and water. Each soap molecule possesses one end that is attracted to water and another end that attaches to oils and dirt, so soap loosens germs from your skin and enables running water to rinse them away. Soap can even dismantle the protective outer layer surrounding certain viruses, which effectively destroys them.

To wash effectively, moisten your hands with clean water, apply soap, and scrub every part of your hands, including the backs, the spaces between your fingers, and the area underneath your fingernails. Continue scrubbing for a minimum of twenty seconds, which is approximately as long as singing a short song twice, and then rinse thoroughly and dry your hands with a clean, uncontaminated towel.

You should consistently wash your hands before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing outdoors or handling animals, since these situations frequently involve contamination. When soap and water are unavailable, a hand sanitizer containing alcohol can provide some protection, although it is considerably less effective on visibly dirty hands. In addition, coughing or sneezing into your elbow rather than your hands reduces the contamination of everything you subsequently touch.

Approximately 175 years ago, a Hungarian physician named Ignaz Semmelweis observed that significantly fewer patients became seriously ill when doctors disinfected their hands, and although many of his colleagues initially rejected his conclusion, handwashing is now considered one of the most essential practices in hospitals throughout the world.

keyWords.example: The soap made lots of bubbles in my hands.

keyWords.definition: to rub something hard to make it clean
keyWords.example: I had to scrub the pot to get the burnt rice off.

keyWords.definition: to move from one place or person to others
keyWords.example: The news about the school trip spread to every class.
Ali stayed home because he was sick with a fever.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to make your own soap
Why some foods are good for you
How washing hands stops germs
How doctors take care of people who are sick
questions.why: The article tells what germs are, how they get on us, and how to wash them away with soap and water.

wrong.A: The article tells how to use soap, not how to make it.
wrong.B: The article is not about food.
wrong.D: The article is about what everyone can do, not about doctors.

questions.stem: How does soap help clean your hands?
options: It lifts germs off your skin.
It makes your hands smell nice.
It turns germs into water.
It makes your skin much too hot for germs to live.
questions.why: The article says soap grabs the germs and lifts them off, and then water takes them away.

wrong.B: Smell is not how soap cleans in the article.
wrong.C: Soap does not turn germs into water.
wrong.D: The article does not say soap makes skin hot.

questions.stem: How long should you scrub your hands?
options: One quick second
Until the water from the tap feels very hot
For one whole hour
As long as a short song sung twice
questions.why: The article says to scrub for about as long as singing a short song twice.

wrong.A: One second is too short to clean well.
wrong.B: The article does not talk about hot water.
wrong.C: An hour is far too long.

questions.stem: Read: "A cough or a sneeze can spread germs." What does spread mean here?
options: Hide in one spot
Move to other places and people
Grow bigger
Wash away
questions.why: A cough sends germs out into the air, so they can move to other people and places.

wrong.A: Spreading is the opposite of staying in one spot.
wrong.C: Spread means move out, not grow.
wrong.D: Coughing does not wash germs away.

questions.stem: What should you do right after you put soap on your wet hands?
options: Dry them with a towel
Eat your lunch
Scrub your hands
Turn off the water and walk away
questions.why: The steps are wet, add soap, scrub, rinse, and dry. Scrubbing comes right after the soap.

wrong.B: Eating is not a step in washing.
wrong.D: You still need to scrub and rinse.

questions.stem: Why is it a good idea to wash your hands before you eat?
options: Germs could get into your mouth.
Food tastes much sweeter when your hands are clean.
Soap helps you feel full.
Your hands get cold when you eat.
questions.why: The article says germs get in when you touch your mouth, and eating means bringing your hands to your mouth.

wrong.B: The article does not say clean hands change the taste.
wrong.C: Soap has nothing to do with feeling full.
wrong.D: The article does not mention cold hands.

questions.stem: Why does the article tell you to cough into your arm and not your hand?
options: Your arm is stronger than your hand.
It makes the cough stop much faster than before.
It is warmer inside your arm.
Your hands touch many things.
questions.why: Hands touch doors and toys, so germs on your hands can get to other people. Your arm does not touch as many things.

wrong.B: Coughing into your arm does not stop the cough.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by saying your hands may have germs even if they look clean?
options: To make readers afraid of their hands
To get readers thinking about germs they cannot see
To show how to dry your hands
To tell a funny story
questions.why: The surprising opening makes readers wonder about invisible germs and want to learn more.

wrong.A: The article gives helpful steps; it does not try to scare readers.
wrong.D: The opening is a fact, not a funny story.

wrong.D: The article says many bacteria are harmless.

questions.stem: Which of these is a time the article recommends washing your hands?
options: Before brushing your hair
After reading a book
After handling animals
Before going to sleep
questions.why: The article lists before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing outdoors or handling animals.

wrong.A: This is not in the article.
wrong.B: This is not in the article.
wrong.D: This is not in the article.

questions.stem: According to the article, what are the two most familiar categories of germs?
options: Molds and yeasts
Bacteria and viruses
Insects and worms
Droplets and oils
questions.why: The article states that the two most familiar categories of germs are bacteria and viruses.

wrong.A: These are not named in the article.
wrong.C: Insects and worms are not microorganisms.
wrong.D: Droplets and oils carry or hold germs; they are not germs.

questions.stem: Read: "The transmission of germs from one person to another occurs remarkably easily." What does transmission mean?
options: The growth of germs
The cleaning of germs
The color of germs
The passing of germs
questions.why: The phrase "from one person to another" shows that transmission means passing something along.

wrong.A: Growth is not described in that sentence.
wrong.B: Cleaning is the opposite of what the sentence describes.

questions.stem: Why is soap able to remove germs from skin?
options: It makes the skin far too slippery for any germs to land on it.
It heats the water so germs cannot survive.
It hides germs under bubbles.
Its molecules attach to water and to oily dirt.
questions.why: Each soap molecule has one end attracted to water and one that attaches to oils and dirt, which loosens germs so water rinses them off.

wrong.A: The article does not explain soap this way.
wrong.C: Bubbles do not hide germs; the soap loosens them.

questions.stem: Many doctors at first rejected Semmelweis's conclusion. What does this suggest?
options: His evidence was false.
New ideas are sometimes doubted even when correct.
Doctors at that time already washed their hands before every patient.
Hospitals did not have water.
questions.why: His idea was rejected at first but is now an essential hospital practice, so it was right despite the early doubt.

wrong.A: Handwashing is now essential in hospitals, so his evidence held up.
wrong.C: If they already washed, his finding would not have been new.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about a lack of water.

questions.stem: Why is touching your face after touching a contaminated surface especially risky?
options: Your face has openings where germs can enter.
Your face always has many more bacteria living on it than your hands do.
Germs on a surface are always harmless.
Touching your face makes soap stop working.
questions.why: The article explains that germs on your skin can enter your body when you rub your eyes or touch your nose or mouth.

wrong.B: The article does not compare these.
wrong.C: The article warns that germs on surfaces can cause infection.
wrong.D: Touching your face does not change how soap works.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with the story of Ignaz Semmelweis?
options: To explain how soap molecules are made
To describe a modern hospital
To show historical evidence that handwashing protects people's health
To compare bacteria and viruses
questions.why: The story shows that handwashing reduced illness and became an essential practice, which supports the article's main point.

wrong.A: Soap molecules are explained earlier, not in the story.
wrong.B: The story happened about 175 years ago.
wrong.D: Bacteria and viruses are described earlier.

HIGH.prompt: Some students say handwashing takes too long and does not matter. Write a persuasive paragraph that uses scientific evidence from the article to convince them otherwise.
checklist: I stated a clear position about handwashing.
I supported it with at least three pieces of scientific or historical evidence from the article.
I addressed the students' concern and ended with a strong conclusion.
